To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

during mitosis, Gin4 becomes hyper-phosphorylated and is assembled into a complex with the septins that includes two copies of Gin4 and that Shs1, one of the septins, is phosphorylated by Gin4 during mito-sis and is likely a target of Gin 4 in vivo.
Gin4 associates with a complex that contains the septins and that the septin Shs1 is a substrate of Gin 4 in vitro and a potential target of Gin 4 kinase activity in the cell.
Gin4 is assembled during mitosis into a complex that includes Shs1, Bni1, Bni4, Nap1, the septins Cdc11, Shs1, Cdc12, and at least one molecule of Cdc28.
In summary, our research is concerned with
how cells regulate cell division, and how defects in this regulation can lead to cancer.
the regulation of mitosis and the cell cycle in general and with the role of the Gin4 kinase in this regulation.
understanding how cells regulate the activity of a protein kinase during the cell division cycle.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
this study identifies the first known targets of Gin4, including the Shs1 subunit of the septin complex, and provides a model for how Gin4 is activated during mitosis.
Gin4 is activated by self-phosphorylation in a complex containing Shs1, and this activation is dependent on Nap1, Cdc28, Cla4, and Elm1.
this paper presents a very nice study of a mitotic protein complex, the Gin4-septins complex, which has a role in cell cycle progression.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the septin complex is the target of a mitotic regulatory network involving Cdc28, Elm1, Nap1 and Gin4.
Gin4, Shs1, and the other septins form a complex that undergoes a mitosis-specific reorganization, with Gin4 and Shs1 playing important roles in this reorganization.
the septin Shs1 plays a role as a target and activator of Gin4, and that Gin4 and Shs1 function together in the regulation of septin localization and function.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the septin complex is a highly dynamic structure, capable of undergoing rapid and regulated changes during mitosis.
the septins are not a simple, static scaffold for other proteins, but rather that they are highly dynamic, and their functions may be controlled by the proteins that they associate with.
Gin4 is assembled during mitosis into a large complex with the septins, Nap1, and Bni5.
